title: 道德經 第五十三章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 53, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 79. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 53 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 益證 (Increase of Evidence). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
使我介然有知，
行於大道，
唯施是畏。

morph.gloss: to cause, to make it so that — here setting up a supposition, 'suppose I were to'
in the least degree, so much as a scrap — 然 makes the word adverbial, as in 超然
slight, a mere sliver (also glossed 'great' by some old commentators)
so, thus — makes what precedes adverbial
to walk, to travel (xíng; háng is 'a row')
on, upon (the all-purpose preposition, standing after its verb)
the Way — and, plainly, a road under the feet; the chapter runs on the double sense
to spread out, to put into effect — officious doing (see the note)
(particle) — NOT 'this': a peg holding the place of the object, which has been moved in front of its verb
to fear, to stand in awe of

sentences.l:
Suppose I had knowing, so much as a scrap of it,
and walked upon the great Way —
it is officious doing alone that I would fear.
sentences.i: If I had even a scrap of understanding and walked the great Way, the one thing I would fear is putting my own hand to things.
sentences.n:
唯施是畏 is a fixed frame worth learning: 唯 X 是 V drags the object X in front of its verb and leaves 是 standing in the gap it came out of. 是 is doing no work of meaning at all here — it is a grammatical peg, not the demonstrative 'this' and certainly not a verb 'to be'. Chapter 51's 莫之命 fronts an object too, but by a different device: there a negative pulls a pronoun object forward and leaves nothing behind in its place.

施 is the crux. Wang Bi glosses the line 唯施為之是畏 — what is feared is 施為, putting one's hand to things, the officious doing this book opposes everywhere — and the English above follows him, as our rule requires. Later scholars read 施 instead as a way of writing 迤 yí, 'to go off sideways', which would make it a fear of straying off the great Way; the very next unit, which complains that people love short-cuts, fits that reading well. Nothing in the text decides it.

介然 is uncertain too. 然 makes it adverbial, as it did in chapter 26's 超然, but 介 was glossed 'slight' by some old commentators and 'great' by others, so the line is either 'if I knew even a little' or 'if I had great knowledge'. We take the first.

sentences.t:
大道甚夷，
而民好徑。

morph.gloss: the Way — and the road itself, which is what 夷 'level' and 徑 'short-cut' are about
level, smooth — ground with nothing raised to catch the foot
to be fond of, to be given to (hào, the verb; not hǎo 'good')
a footpath, a short cut cross-country — as against the highroad

sentences.l:
The great Way is very level,
and yet the people love short-cuts.
sentences.i: The great Way runs perfectly level, and still people are fond of by-ways.
sentences.n:
徑 is a track worn across country by people cutting a corner — quicker, narrower, and not the road. The whole complaint of the chapter is in the contrast.

夷 was 'the featureless' in chapter 14, the name given there to what cannot be seen; in chapter 41's 夷道若纇 it was already 'level', as here — flat ground with nothing raised for the foot to catch.

好 is hào, the verb 'to be given to', which you met in chapter 30's 其事好還.

morph.gloss: the court, the ruler's palace (cháo — NOT zhāo 'morning', its reading in chapter 23)

sentences.l: The court is swept very clean,
sentences.n:
Wang Bi glosses 朝 as 宮室, the palace buildings, and 除 as 潔好, 'clean and fine'. So the picture is a court kept spotless while everything under it goes to ruin — the three units that follow supply the ruin.

除 has a second sense, 'cleared away, stripped', and some read the line that way instead: the court itself in decay. Wang Bi's gloss is the reason we do not.

sentences.l:
the fields very rank with weeds,
the granaries very empty;
sentences.i: the fields choked with weeds, the granaries standing empty;
sentences.n: Three 甚 in a row, one to a clause, and no word anywhere for 'while' or 'but'. The parallel does all the joining — set the clean palace beside the weeds and the empty granaries and the argument is made without being stated. This language leaves the joints open far more often than English can bear.

sentences.t:
服文綵，
帶利劍，
厭飲食，
財貨有餘；
是為盜夸。
非道也哉！

morph.gloss: figured silks — patterned and coloured stuff, the dress of rank
to wear at the belt, to gird on
to have had one's fill of, to be glutted with (not the modern 'to dislike')
to eat; food (shí; sì would be 'to feed another')
goods and wealth — property, the kind that is counted and hoarded
the robber's swagger — the brag of a thief; the text coins the phrase and names it
to boast, to swell, to make a show
is not (negating a noun predicate — Classical Chinese has no verb 'to be')

sentences.l:
wearing figured silks,
girt with a sharp sword,
sated with food and drink,
goods and wealth in surplus —
this counts as the robber's swagger.
Not the Way!
sentences.i: dressed in figured silk, a keen sword at the belt, sated with food and drink, and a surplus of goods and wealth: this is a robber's swagger. It is not the Way!
sentences.n:
Han Feizi, writing in the third century BC and the earliest commentator we have on this book, quotes this passage and reads the phrase as 盜竽 rather than 盜夸. The 竽 was the big reed-pipe that led an ensemble and gave the others their pitch, so on his reading the man described is the chief robber the lesser robbers take their note from. The two characters were close in sound, our edition prints 夸 'to boast', and the choice is old either way.

非道也哉 stacks two final particles: 也 sets the statement down flat, 哉 lifts it into an exclamation. The book almost never raises its voice; this is one of the few places where it does.

厭 is a false friend. In modern Chinese it is dislike; here it is the older sense, to have one's fill to the point of surfeit.

非道 closes the chapter on the character that opened it. 大道 in the first two units is a road under the feet; 道 here is the Way. Chinese has one word for both, and the whole complaint is built on that — a highroad kept level, and men who will not keep to it.
